as_told: If you drop a frog into boiling water, it jumps out at once. If you put it in cool water and heat the water slowly, it does not notice the danger. It stays in the water and is boiled to death.
lesson: People do not notice or react to a danger that grows slowly, until it is too late.
what_happened: In 1869 the physiologist Friedrich Goltz heated frogs in water to study where the frog's mind sits. A frog whose head had been cut off sat still until it died. A frog with its brain but with its eyes blinded grew restless at about 25 degrees C, tried hard to escape and died at about 42 degrees C. In a second run, a frog whose forebrain had been cut away jumped out of the vessel six times. In 1872 Heinzmann reported that even normal frogs could be heated to death without moving if the heating was very slow, but Goltz and Tarchanow had found the opposite. Sedgwick's review of 1882 calls the motionless frog a 'brainless frog' and records that the reports on normal frogs disagree. In Goltz's runs the frogs died of heat at about 42 degrees C, or went stiff at 56 degrees C; none was boiled.
false_part: The frog that is recorded sitting still until it died had no brain; in the first experiment, frogs that kept the brain stem tried hard to escape, and one jumped out.

lesson_verdict.why: A large study of social media posts found that people quickly stop remarking on unusual temperatures, which fits the idea that slow change goes unnoticed. But the same study found that people still feel the bad effects, and it does not show that people fail to act in time.

source.what: Moore, Obradovich, Lehner and Baylis, 'Rapidly declining remarkability of temperature anomalies may obscure public perception of climate change', PNAS 116(11):4905-4910 (2019)
source.quote: The declining noteworthiness of historically extreme temperatures is not accompanied by a decline in the negative sentiment that they induce

search_steps: Open Library full-text search for "frog" "heated" "slowly" "boiled": the first request failed (connection reset); a second search for "frog" "boiled" "without moving" gave 50,301 hits, mostly joke and trick books; nothing older than 1878 and nothing on point.

Archive.org search for E. W. Scripture, The New Psychology (1897): saved the djvu text of cu31924024541298. Page 300 says a live frog 'can actually be boiled without a movement if the water is heated slowly enough' and cites Heinzmann 1872, Fratscher 1875 and Sedgwick 1882. This is a retelling, used as a lead.

English Wikipedia talk page 'Talk:Boiling frog/sources' lists Goltz 1869, Heinzmann 1872, Foster 1873, Fratscher 1875, Sedgwick 1882, Scripture 1897 and Morgan 1904, with archive.org identifiers. Used only as a lead.
Saved Sedgwick 1882 (archive.org studiesfrombiol00martgoog). Pages 386-391 describe Goltz's experiment and Heinzmann's contrary result.

Saved Goltz 1869 (archive.org b29291069). Pages 127-130 give the experiment: the brainless frog sits still until heat rigor at 56 degrees C; the blinded frog with its brain struggles from about 25 degrees C and dies at about 42 degrees C; in a second run a frog with its forebrain cut away jumped out six times. The whole first run took about 10 minutes, so the heating was not very slow.

Heinzmann 1872 (Pflügers Archiv vol. 6, pp. 222-236): archive.org search found no scan of 1872 volumes; the Springer copy is behind a paywall. Not read; known only through Sedgwick's summary, so not quoted.
Fratscher 1875 (Jenaische Zeitschrift): only a snippet view is reported on Google Books. Not read.
HathiTrust full-text search: refused with a Cloudflare check (403). Google Books API: refused with 429; did not retry.
Free newspaper archives: Chronicling America (loc.gov) refused with 403 and Papers Past refused with a bot check (Incapsula); did not retry. Trove needs an API key and was not tried.
Goltz's footnote on p. 127 points to his earlier report in Königsberger medicinische Jahrbücher, vol. 1, p. 218. An archive.org search for that journal found nothing; not read.
Teller correction: Goltz's own account already shows that frogs with a brain try to escape; no later correction by Goltz, Heinzmann or Scripture was found.
Lesson source: saved Moore et al. 2019 from PubMed Central (PMC6421414). The escholarship PDF and the Europe PMC PDF returned HTML instead; PNAS returned 403.
confidence_note: Heinzmann (1872) claimed that normal frogs also stayed still under very slow heating; I could not read his paper, so the question of whether an intact frog can be heated to death without escaping is not settled by the sources I hold. What the sources I hold show is that the classic motionless frog was brainless, and that Goltz's frogs with a brain (one blinded, one without its forebrain) tried to escape when heated over about 10 minutes. No fully intact frog heated very slowly appears in the sources I read. The class 'changed' rests on this; if Heinzmann's result is sound, part of the story for intact frogs would be 'unsupported' rather than false. Modern biologists are often quoted saying frogs jump out, but I found no published paper by them and did not use those quotes.
